# Gaming / Entertainment

**Page type:** detail page (one h2 per pitfall, each followed by a two-column obj-table row: text left 50%, canvas right 50%)
**HTML title tag:** Gaming / Entertainment - Domain-Specific Data Pitfalls

**Subtitle:** Data pitfalls unique to games, interactive entertainment, and player behavior analytics

## Callout (philosophy box)

**Core tension:** Gaming data is generated by systems that actively shape behavior. Matchmaking, reward schedules, and content gating all create the data you later analyze. Confusing system-induced patterns with player preferences is the fundamental error in gaming analytics.

## Engagement Does Not Equal Enjoyment

**Obj-title:** The Slot Machine Fallacy

High session time and frequency are reflexively treated as success metrics. But slot machines are extremely "engaging" while users report low satisfaction. Dark patterns (variable reward schedules, loss aversion triggers, FOMO mechanics) inflate engagement without creating genuine enjoyment.

- **Symptom:** DAU and session length look great, so the dashboard reads as a healthy game
- **Late signal:** NPS stays low and 30-day churn runs high, contradicting the engagement numbers
- **Root cause:** Compulsion loops drive short-term engagement and long-term player resentment
- **Fix:** Pair engagement metrics with satisfaction surveys and long-term retention cohorts
- **Regret probe:** Ask "Did you mean to play that long?" — regret, not time, separates fun from compulsion

## Whale Dependence Distorts "Average User" Models

**Obj-title:** The Pareto Revenue Problem

In free-to-play games, the top 1% of spenders ("whales") typically generate 50%+ of revenue. Models trained on average user behavior completely miss the economic reality. Optimizing for the median player may actively harm the experience for whales, destroying revenue.

- **Symptom:** A/B test shows the feature improves average engagement, yet revenue drops 20%
- **Root cause:** The feature annoyed whales, who spend 100-1000x more than the median player
- **Fix:** Segment every analysis by spending tier before reading any aggregate result
- **No naked averages:** Never report an average without stating the revenue distribution behind it
- **Separate models:** Build distinct models for whales, dolphins, minnows, and free players

## Content Lifecycle Decay Invalidates Early Models

**Obj-title:** The Novelty Spike Trap

New content (maps, characters, events) creates massive engagement spikes that decay rapidly. A model trained on week-1 data will systematically overpredict future engagement. This leads to over-investment in content that appears successful but normalizes quickly.

- **Symptom:** Forecasts consistently overestimate engagement for content older than 2 weeks
- **Root cause:** Training data dominated by the novelty period; the decay curve is never modeled
- **Fix:** Wait 4+ weeks after release before training any engagement model on new content
- **Model the decay:** Fit the decay curve explicitly instead of treating week-1 levels as the baseline
- **Steady state only:** Use post-decay steady-state data for long-term engagement predictions

### Visualization (canvas `canvas3`, 720×260)

- **Model prediction:** horizontal dashed 8/5 `#e74c3c` width-2 line at 92%, labeled (bold 13px `#e74c3c`): "Model prediction (trained on W0-W1)".
- **Curve label (bold 13px, `#1a5276`):** "Actual engagement".
- **Overprediction zone:** `rgba(231,76,60,0.12)` rectangle between the prediction line and the ~15% steady state over the right 70% of the plot, labeled (12px `#e74c3c`, centered): "Overprediction zone".

## Matchmaking Creates the Data It Measures

**Obj-title:** The Endogenous Data Problem

Matchmaking systems decide who plays whom. Bad matchmaking (stomps, mismatches) generates frustration data, not preference data. You cannot learn what players want from data generated by a broken system, because the system itself caused the negative outcomes.

- **Symptom:** The preference model concludes "players prefer short matches" from match-length data
- **Real explanation:** Those short matches are just stomps ending early, not matches players enjoyed
- **Root cause:** The matchmaker created 80-20 skill mismatches, so the data records system failure
- **Fix:** Train preference models only on data drawn from skill-balanced, non-stomp matches
- **Causal inference:** Separate matchmaker effects from genuine player preference before believing either
- **Controlled test:** Run experiments with known-fair matchmaking to get uncontaminated preference data

### Visualization (canvas `canvas4`, 720×260)

Two side-by-side win-rate histograms: unimodal (good) vs bimodal (bad).

- **Panels:** each 310×180; left at x=40, right at x=380, top y=50. Panel titles (bold 15px, centered at y=20): "Good Matchmaking" in `#27ae60`; "Bad Matchmaking" in `#e74c3c`. Subtitle under each (12px `#666`): "Win Rate Distribution".
- **Histogram bars** (15 bins across 0%–100% win rate, `#1a5276` baseline axis, 11px `#666` x labels "0%", "50%", "100%" plus "Win Rate"):
  - Good (fill `rgba(39,174,96,0.6)`), tight normal around 50%: `[2, 4, 8, 14, 22, 35, 50, 65, 50, 35, 22, 14, 8, 4, 2]`
  - Bad (fill `rgba(231,76,60,0.6)`), bimodal stomps: `[35, 50, 40, 25, 12, 6, 4, 6, 12, 25, 40, 50, 35, 20, 10]`
- **50% marker:** dashed 4/3 `#1a5276` vertical line at the good panel's midpoint.
- **Annotations (12px, centered below each panel):** green: "Balanced: data reflects" / "true player preferences"; red: "Stomps (80-20): data reflects" / "frustration, not preferences".

## Smurf Accounts Contaminate New Player Data

**Obj-title:** The Bimodal Beginner Problem

Expert players create new accounts ("smurfs") to dominate lower-skill lobbies. These accounts appear in your "new player" cohort but perform at expert level. Any model of new player behavior, onboarding effectiveness, or skill progression is contaminated by this population.

- **Symptom:** The "new player" skill distribution is bimodal rather than clustered at beginner level
- **Blind A/B tests:** Onboarding experiments show no effect at all on the high-skill sub-population
- **Root cause:** In competitive games, 10-25% of "new" accounts are smurfs run by expert players
- **Fix:** Detect smurfs from behavioral signals — key rebinding, APM, menu navigation speed
- **Cohort hygiene:** Exclude detected smurfs from new-player analyses and cohort them separately
- **Bad proxy:** Never treat account age as a proxy for a player's actual skill or experience

### Visualization (canvas `canvas5`, 720×260)

Expected unimodal vs actual bimodal skill-rating density curves for "new" accounts.

- **Axes:** `#1a5276` width-2 L axes, origin (90,210), plot 560 × 160. X label (14px): "Performance Level (Skill Rating)" with 12px `#666` category labels "Beginner" (20%), "Intermediate" (50%), "Expert" (80%). Y label (rotated): "# of "New" Accounts".
- **Expected curve:** dashed 6/4 `#27ae60` width 2 — Gaussian centered at 20% of the axis, sigma² = 144 (on a 0–100 scale), peak scaled to 90% of plot height.
- **Actual curve:** solid `#e74c3c` width 3 — mixture: 0.82 × Gaussian(mean 20, sigma² 120) + 0.25 × Gaussian(mean 80, sigma² 60), same scaling. Beginner peak filled `rgba(39,174,96,0.1)` (x 0–50%); smurf bump filled `rgba(231,76,60,0.15)` (x 55–100%).
- **Curve labels (bold 13px):** "Expected (unimodal)" in green near the left peak; "Actual (bimodal)" in red mid-plot.
- **Smurf annotation (12px, `#e74c3c`, centered at ~80% x):** "Smurf contamination" / "(~15-25% of "new" accounts)", with a red arrow pointing down to the smurf peak.
- **Legend (12px, top of chart):** dashed green line sample "Expected: real beginners only"; solid red line sample "Actual: beginners + smurfs".
